The round trip starts at A (outlined) and follows the accent arrows A, B, C, D, E, back to A, visiting every site once; the chords are faded. The card shows the route and its cost 2 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 12." width="100%"} The traveling salesperson problem asks for the cheapest round trip that visits each of a set of locations exactly once. Here the graph does not need to be complete: the route moves between consecutive stops along shortest paths, so the problem is solved on the *metric closure* (see `metric_closure()`) and the returned walk may pass through other nodes on the way. The problem is NP-hard, so the methods are heuristics that give good, but not always optimal, routes. Typical uses are delivery and service routes, drilling and printing orders, and sequencing samples or jobs. Methods: - `"christofides"` (default for undirected graphs): at most 1.5 times the optimal cost. - `"greedy"`: nearest neighbor from the first node; fast, no guarantee. - `"simulated_annealing"` and `"threshold_accepting"`: start from the greedy route and improve it with random moves (`"threshold_accepting"` is the default for directed graphs, where Christofides does not apply). Use `seed=` for reproducible results. - `"asadpour"`: Asadpour et al.'s randomized rounding of a linear programming bound, for one-way streets and other asymmetric costs; within $O(\log k / \log \log k)$ of optimal (with high probability) for $k$ stops, and often much closer. Use `seed=` for reproducible results. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Union[int, str]] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : The stops to visit (IDs or labels). If `None` (default), every node. [cycle]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), return to the start. If `False`, return a path instead: the most expensive leg of the round trip is removed. [method]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : One of the methods above. If `None` (default), `"christofides"` for undirected and `"threshold_accepting"` for directed graphs. [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to use edge weights as travel costs. If `None` (default), follows the graph's `weighted` flag; with `False` every edge costs `1`. Weights must be non-negative. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed for the local search methods and `"asadpour"`. [max_iter]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[10]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Local search only: stop after this many outer rounds without an improvement. [n_inner]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[100]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Local search only: moves tried per outer round. [move]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["1-1"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Local search only: `"1-1"` (default) swaps two stops, `"1-0"` moves one stop to a new position. [temperature]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Local search only: the starting temperature for simulated annealing (default `100`) or the starting threshold for threshold accepting (default `1`). These are in units of edge weight, so scale them with your weights. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The walk as node IDs. With `cycle=True`, the first and last node are the same. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a stop cannot be reached from another, a weight is negative, `method="christofides"` is used on a directed graph, or an argument is invalid. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Distances between stops are computed with Dijkstra's algorithm from every stop. On that complete, metric instance, Christofides' algorithm (1976) builds a minimum spanning tree, adds a minimum-weight perfect matching on its odd-degree nodes (Edmonds' blossom algorithm), walks an Eulerian circuit of the union, and skips repeated nodes; the triangle inequality makes the result at most $\tfrac{3}{2}$ times optimal, in $O(k^3)$ time for $k$ stops. Simulated annealing accepts a worse route with probability $e^{-\Delta / T}$ and cools $T$ by 1% per round; threshold accepting accepts any move worse by at most the threshold, which shrinks by 10% per round with an accepted move. Both follow NetworkX's design, but unlike NetworkX they leave the current route unchanged when a move is rejected. The `"asadpour"` method (Asadpour, Goemans, Madry, Oveis Gharan and Saberi, 2017) first solves the Held-Karp relaxation: the cheapest fractional assignment of arcs with one unit leaving and entering each stop and at least one unit leaving every subset of stops. It is solved exactly by a dense two-phase simplex method, adding the subset constraints as cutting planes found by minimum cuts. If the optimum is a tour, it is returned (it is optimal). Otherwise the solution is symmetrized and scaled by $(k - 1) / k$, a maximum entropy distribution of spanning trees matching those edge marginals is fitted, and $2 \lceil \ln k \rceil$ trees are drawn from it (Wilson's algorithm). The cheapest, with each edge oriented its cheaper way, is made Eulerian by a minimum-cost flow that balances in- and out-degrees, and its Eulerian circuit is shortcut into the tour. NetworkX's `asadpour_atsp()` follows the same steps but reaches the relaxation by Held and Karp's ascent over enumerated 1-arborescences, which is much slower (seconds already at 6 stops, against milliseconds here for 25), and it picks the sampled tree and orients its edges by the tree distribution's weights instead of the travel costs. The method also works on undirected graphs, where NetworkX raises an error, but Christofides is the better choice there. The simplex tableau has $k^2$ columns, so this is meant for at most a few dozen stops. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Five sites linked by roads, weighted by travel time. The route visits every site and returns to the start, for a total of 2 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 12: ::: {#85ef6394 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(weighted=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) g.add_edges( [ ("A", "B", 2.0), ("B", "C", 2.0), ("C", "D", 3.0), ("D", "E", 2.0), ("E", "A", 3.0), ("A", "C", 4.0), ("B", "E", 3.0), ] ) route = g.traveling_salesman() [g.get_label_from_id(n) for n in route] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E', 'A'] ``` ::: ::: Only some nodes may need a visit. With stops A and D, the round trip passes through B and C (which are not stops) in both directions, because the path is the only way between them: ::: {#8d9b844a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} path = ec.Graph(weighted=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) path.add_edges([("A", "B", 1.0), ("B", "C", 1.0), ("C", "D", 1.0)]) [path.get_label_from_id(n) for n in path.traveling_salesman(nodes=["A", "D"])] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'C', 'B', 'A'] ``` ::: ::: With `cycle=False` the most expensive leg of the round trip (E-A or C-D, weight 3) is dropped, leaving a one-way route: ::: {#2ff86a71 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} [g.get_label_from_id(n) for n in g.traveling_salesman(cycle=False, method="greedy")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['D', 'E', 'A', 'B', 'C'] ``` ::: ::: On a directed graph, travel costs can depend on the direction. Going clockwise around these three sites costs 2 per leg, but counterclockwise only 1, which the `"asadpour"` method finds: ::: {#ce8c8b5b .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} oneway = ec.Graph(directed=True, weighted=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) oneway.add_edges( [ ("A", "B", 2.0), ("B", "C", 2.0), ("C", "A", 2.0), ("A", "C", 1.0), ("C", "B", 1.0), ("B", "A", 1.0), ] ) [oneway.get_label_from_id(n) for n in oneway.traveling_salesman(method="asadpour")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ['A', 'C', 'B', 'A'] ``` ::: :::
